notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses right after Aaron's two sons died for approaching God the wrong way. God gave these new instructions to protect Aaron and future priests from making the same fatal mistake. It showed how holy God is and why a proper way to approach Him was needed.

God warned that Aaron must not enter the Most Holy Place behind the curtain whenever he pleased, or he would die. The Lord's presence appeared in a cloud above the mercy seat, making that inner room sacred. The high priest could only enter on God's chosen day and by God's exact rules.

Aaron had to bring a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering before he could enter the sacred area. These animals were offered for Aaron and his family. Before he could serve as a go-between for the people, his own sins had to be covered.

Aaron had to bathe with water and put on plain linen clothing instead of his usual ornate golden robes. These humble white garments showed simplicity, purity, and lowliness before the Lord on a day of mourning for sin. Washing first was a reminder that anyone serving God must be clean.

The community of Israel gave Aaron two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering. These animals belonged to the whole nation to deal with their shared guilt. Even though the two goats served two different roles, together they formed one single sin offering.

Aaron presented the bull to make atonement for himself and his priestly family. Atonement means making things right between God and sinners by covering their guilt. Because Aaron was a flawed human being, he had to be forgiven first before he could lead the people.

Aaron brought the two goats to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to stand before the Lord. Presenting them at the doorway showed that both animals were fully dedicated to God's service. This prepared them for the special choice that was about to take place.
Aaron cast lots over the two goats to discover God's purpose for each one. One lot was for the Lord, and the other was for the scapegoat. Casting lots left the final decision entirely in God's hands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars translate the Hebrew word Azazel as the name of a desert demon or as a word meaning complete removal or rough terrain.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars traditionally translate the word as the emissary or sent-away goat, while noting that some interpret it as referring to an evil spirit in the wilderness.

notes.meaning: Aaron brought forward the goat chosen by lot for the Lord and prepared it as a sin offering. This animal was to be sacrificed on the altar so its blood could pay the penalty for the people's sins. Its death satisfied God's justice and opened the way for forgiveness.

The other goat was kept alive before the Lord and sent away into the wilderness. This living goat was used to make atonement by carrying the people's guilt far away from the camp. It pictured sins being completely removed so they would never be remembered against Israel.

Aaron brought the bull and slaughtered it as a sin offering for himself and his household. He confessed his own sins and those of the priests over the animal before killing it. This showed that even God's chief priest was a sinner who needed blood to cover his guilt.

Aaron took a fire pan filled with burning coals from the bronze altar and two handfuls of finely ground incense. He carried both items inside the veil into the Most Holy Place. This action prepared the room before any blood was brought in.

Aaron placed the incense on the hot coals so a fragrant cloud of smoke quickly covered the mercy seat. This sweet smoke screened the direct glory of God's presence above the ark so Aaron would not die. It also pictures the prayers that rise up to God on behalf of His people.

Aaron dipped his finger into the bull's blood and sprinkled it on the front of the mercy seat, and seven times on the floor before it. Sprinkling the blood showed that God accepts sinners only through a life given in sacrifice. The number seven stood for a complete and perfect cleansing.

Aaron went out to slaughter the people's sin offering goat and brought its blood behind the veil. He sprinkled the goat's blood on and before the mercy seat just as he had done with the bull's blood. This brought cleansing and pardon for the sins of the entire nation.

Aaron made atonement for the Most Holy Place and the Tent of Meeting because the sins of Israel had polluted the sanctuary. The holy tent stood right in the middle of an imperfect camp and gathered moral uncleanness over the year. Cleansing the sacred space allowed God to keep dwelling among His people.

No other priest or worshipper was permitted inside the Tent of Meeting while Aaron made atonement in the inner room. Aaron had to do this sacred work alone to show deep respect for God's majesty. It reminded Israel that only their appointed mediator could stand before God for them.

Aaron came out to the altar before the Lord to cleanse it as well. He took blood from both the bull and the goat and smeared it on all four horns of the altar. This act purified the very place where daily worship was offered to God.

Aaron sprinkled the blood on the altar seven times with his finger to wash away the stains of Israel's uncleanness. This set the altar apart once more as holy and pleasing to God. It ensured that future sacrifices would be offered on a clean altar.

When Aaron finished purifying the inner room, the holy tent, and the altar, he brought the living goat forward. The sacred places were now restored and clean before God. The second part of the ceremony could begin to remove the people's guilt directly.

Aaron pressed both hands onto the goat's head and openly confessed all the sins and rebellions of Israel. This showed that the nation's guilt was transferred to the animal as their substitute. An appointed man then took charge of the goat to lead it away from the camp.

The live goat carried all the sins of Israel out into a lonely and uninhabited land. The man released the goat in the desert so it would never return. This dramatic act showed the people that God had carried their sins away into forgetfulness.

Aaron went back into the Tent of Meeting, took off his simple linen garments, and left them there. Those clothes had been set apart only for the inner room ceremony. Leaving them behind marked the end of the most solemn part of the day's ritual.

Aaron washed his body in a holy area and put his regular high priest robes back on. He then went outside to offer the burnt offerings for himself and the people. These offerings showed full dedication to God and restored fellowship with Him.

Aaron burned the rich fat of the sin offerings on the bronze altar in the courtyard. The fat was considered the richest part of the animal and was reserved entirely for God. Burning it completed the sacrifice for sin and showed God's acceptance of the offering.

The man who led the scapegoat into the wilderness had to wash his clothes and bathe before returning to the camp. Handling an animal loaded with the people's sins made him ritually unclean. Washing kept defilement from spreading back into the community.

The bodies of the bull and goat whose blood had entered the Most Holy Place were carried outside the camp and burned completely. Priests were not allowed to eat any part of these sacrifices. Burning them outside the camp showed that the sin they represented was entirely removed from God's presence.

The person who burned the carcasses also had to wash his clothes and bathe in water before entering the camp. Because he handled the remains of the sin offerings, he carried ceremonial uncleanness. Cleaning himself allowed him to safely rejoin the community.

God commanded this day to be kept every year on the tenth day of the seventh month as a permanent law. All native Israelites and foreigners living among them had to stop work and humble themselves through fasting. It was a nationwide day of serious repentance before God.

On this special day, the priest made atonement to cleanse the people from all their sins before the Lord. God promised that everyone who took part with a sincere heart would stand clean in His presence. It gave the whole nation a fresh start for the coming year.

This day was a Sabbath of complete rest where all regular labor had to stop. The people were to spend their time denying themselves and seeking God's mercy. It was an enduring rule designed to teach them that forgiveness is God's gift, not something earned by work.

Whenever a new high priest was anointed to succeed his father, he was required to perform these same ceremonies. He too had to put on the sacred white linen garments for the service. The high priest's role was lifelong and passed down through the family line.

The high priest made atonement for the inner sanctuary, the sacred tent, the altar, the priests, and the entire assembly. This verse summarizes the full reach of the day's work. Every place of worship and every group of people was covered and made clean before God.

This annual ceremony was to be kept once every year as a lasting law for Israel. Repeating it year after year showed that animal blood could not remove sin once and for all. Aaron obeyed every word and carried out the service exactly as the Lord had commanded Moses.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching sees this yearly ritual as pointing to Christ's sacrifice on the Cross, which is renewed daily in an unbloody manner on the altar during the Mass.
